title: End of apartheid
summary: From the unbanning of the ANC on 2 February 1990 to Nelson Mandela's inauguration on 10 May 1994, South Africa dismantled its system of legalised racial domination by negotiation, amid severe political violence.
card: President F. W. de Klerk lifted the ban on the ANC and other liberation movements on 2 February 1990, and Nelson Mandela left prison nine days later after about 27 years. Talks produced an interim constitution, and the first election open to all races on 27 April 1994 gave the ANC 62.65% of the vote. The same years saw roughly 14,000 politically related deaths, and the later Truth and Reconciliation Commission tried to record them.
what: Apartheid was the system of legally enforced racial classification and separation that South Africa's National Party government introduced after taking office in 1948; the Population Registration Act and Group Areas Act of 1950 were among its pillars. Its end came as a negotiated transition between 1990 and 1994, not a single event. On 2 February 1990 President F. W. de Klerk told Parliament in Cape Town that the African National Congress (ANC), the Pan Africanist Congress, the South African Communist Party and fifty-eight other organisations were unbanned, that political prisoners would be freed and that exiles could return. Nelson Mandela, jailed since 1962 and sentenced to life at the 1964 Rivonia Trial, left Victor Verster Prison near Paarl on 11 February 1990 after about 27 years. The ANC suspended its armed struggle in August 1990, and a series of laws were repealed in 1991. The multiparty Convention for a Democratic South Africa (CODESA) opened in December 1991, broke down over majority rule and regional powers, and resumed in other forms. White voters alone were asked on 17 March 1992 whether reform should continue, and 68.7% said yes. Talks nearly collapsed after the Boipatong massacre (17 June 1992), the shooting of marchers at Bisho (7 September 1992) and the assassination of the Communist Party leader Chris Hani (10 April 1993). Negotiators at Kempton Park agreed an interim constitution with a bill of rights on 18 November 1993; it took effect on 27 April 1994, the first day of South Africa's first election open to all adults. The ANC won 62.65% of the vote, and Mandela was inaugurated on 10 May 1994 at the head of a government of national unity. The transition was violent: the Truth and Reconciliation Commission recorded a dramatic escalation of killings and cites other sources for some 14,000 politically related deaths between mid-1990 and April 1994. Scholars differ on why the government chose to negotiate, on how far a covert "third force" drove the violence, and on whether the "end" is the 1990 unbannings, the 1994 election or the later constitution; this record spans 2 February 1990 to 10 May 1994.

uncertainty.note: Both bounds are exact dates, but the choice of bounds is a convention: the process is bounded here by De Klerk's unbanning speech and Mandela's inauguration. Some accounts date the end of apartheid to the election of 27 April 1994 or to the 1996 constitution; the Truth and Reconciliation Commission treats 10 May 1994 as the close of its mandate period.

how: The sequence began with pressure on the government that built up through the 1980s: township revolt, a state of emergency, bank loan withdrawal in 1984, token Western sanctions from 1987, and the military setback at Cuito Cuanavale in 1988. Secret contacts between officials and the exiled ANC started in 1987, and ministers met Mandela in prison from 1988. After P. W. Botha was replaced by De Klerk in 1989, the government announced the unbannings on 2 February 1990 and freed Mandela nine days later. Bilateral talks produced the Groote Schuur Minute (May 1990) and the Pretoria Minute (August 1990), after which the ANC suspended its armed struggle. CODESA opened in December 1991 with twenty organisations and stalled over majority rule and regional powers. Violence then escalated: Boipatong (17 June 1992) led the ANC to leave the talks, and after Bisho (7 September 1992) and a Record of Understanding between the ANC and the government, negotiations resumed with the government abandoning its informal alliance with the Inkatha Freedom Party. Inkatha, homeland rulers and the white right grouped as the Freedom Alliance and walked out in July 1993. A Transitional Executive Council was installed in December 1993. The interim constitution of 18 November 1993 set out a bill of rights, proportional representation, a five-year government of national unity and an amnesty for politically motivated crimes. In March 1994 the Bophuthatswana government fell after the white right intervened, and Ciskei's collapsed two weeks later. The Freedom Alliance was brought into the election shortly before 27 April 1994.
why_it_matters: The transition ended the legal exclusion of the Black majority from South African citizenship and the vote: some 19.7 million ballots were cast in April 1994 in the first election open to all adults, and the interim constitution created a Constitutional Court and a justiciable bill of rights that the 1996 constitution inherited. It also showed that a minority regime with a working army and economy could be brought to negotiate its own end, which influenced debate on peaceful transitions elsewhere; the Nobel Committee cited it as a model for resolving other deep-rooted conflicts. The settlement had costs. The negotiated compromise protected civil servants' jobs and property rights and dropped ANC plans for nationalisation, and Lodge argues that the ANC has since dominated politics as a one-party-dominant system. Political violence killed thousands, and its covert networks were never fully exposed; the amnesty clause led directly to the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, whose 21,000 victim statements are now the main public record of the apartheid era. Without the unbannings of February 1990, or if the talks had collapsed after Boipatong or Hani's assassination, South Africa could have faced the civil war that Inkatha's negotiator threatened, and the 1994 election might not have taken place with the participation of nearly all parties. Today's inequality in land, income and schooling, which the settlement did not undo, is still measured against the apartheid-era divisions.

related.title: National Party election victory of 1948 and the first apartheid laws
related.because: The 1948 National Party government introduced the system of racial classification and separation that the 1990-94 negotiations dismantled.

related.title: Soweto uprising
related.because: Township revolt from 1976 and its repression helped build the internal unrest and international condemnation that the US State Department and Lodge both cite as reasons for the government's later shift.

related.title: Battle of Cuito Cuanavale
related.because: Lodge records that the South African military lost air supremacy there in 1988, which led generals to advise withdrawal from Namibia and raised the cost of the old security strategy.
The collapse of Communist governments in 1989 ended key sources of the ANC's foreign support, which De Klerk took as a sign that the ANC could be negotiated with from strength.

related.title: South African general election of 1994
related.because: The interim constitution and the negotiated timetable fixed the date and rules for the first election open to voters of all races.

related.title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission
related.because: The interim constitution required an amnesty for politically motivated acts, and the 1995 Act created the commission to investigate violations and hear amnesty applications.

perspectives.account: De Klerk's government began the transition because sanctions and credit limits were damaging a stalled economy, because it could contain the ANC militarily but could not win consent from Black South Africans, and because the end of Communist governments seemed to weaken the ANC. Its aim was a power-sharing settlement, built partly on an alliance with Inkatha, in which whites kept a decisive role; it did not intend to hand over majority rule.

perspectives.holder: Office of the Historian, U.S. Department of State
perspectives.account: Years of violent internal protest, weakening white commitment, international economic and cultural sanctions, economic difficulty and the end of the Cold War together brought down white minority rule; the relaxation of Cold War tension also helped end the Angola conflict.

The Commission found little evidence of a centrally directed, formal "third force", but found that networks of current and former security-force operatives, often with right-wing elements or parts of the IFP, were involved in fomenting violence. It also held the ANC responsible for killings and attacks on opponents, partly through self-defence units, and held the KwaZulu Police overwhelmingly biased towards the IFP. The earlier Goldstone Commission had initially found no evidence of a third force and blamed political intolerance, while monitoring groups and newspapers continued to allege one.

perspectives.holder: Women's organisations and the historian Loraine Maritz
perspectives.account: Women were absent from the first CODESA negotiating teams, which led the ANC Women's League to set up the Women's National Coalition in 1992 (about 100 organisations, around thirteen of them Afrikaner women's groups) to draw up a Women's Charter for the constitution. Maritz argues that party politics, practical problems and hostility strained the Coalition and Afrikaner women's place in it.

audience_note: This record describes massacres, killings of civilians by police, soldiers, paramilitaries and unknown gunmen, and a political assassination, as well as the racial system of apartheid. It contains no graphic images, but the linked records on Sebokeng, Boipatong, Bisho and Hani may.

importance.justification: The dismantling of the last formal white-minority regime in Africa and the first non-racial election in South Africa, with global influence on debates about transitions from authoritarian rule.

reviewer_note: Least sure of the exact CODESA opening date and the Record of Understanding date (sources here give only month or year), of the SAHO-hosted election and referendum figures (secondary compilations of IEC data), and of Khoisan and other Indigenous voices, which I did not find sourced.
